newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup - Free trade zeal.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup - Free trade zeal.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
Free trade is a bit like religion.
Get some world leaders together to talk trade and suddenly you have a group of free trade evangelists.
Prime Minister John Howard is our case in point.
Shortly after winning office, Howard articulated what he called his hard-headed approach to tariff reductions.

"There are a lot of people in Australia who believe that we give away by way of industry initiatives (and that) there has to be some reciprocity and I think that is very understandable, reciprocity in a proper sense," he said.
"But I think it's also fair to say that we see intrinsic benefits, cost wise, for our efficient industries in a low tariff regime."
In other words, Howard was making his support for continued reduction in tariffs conditional upon a quid pro quo from trading partners.
And just before he left for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) meeting in the Philippines and soon after his arrival he was travelling the same road.
He said national interest rather than economic theory should be the guide to future reform.
He went on to describe the debate over the government's stance on tariff reductions as "absurd" and "infantile."

"I think we waste an enormous amount of energy in Australia, may I say so, both at a political level and an analytical and journalistic level in the nuances of how free (or) non-free-trade somebody is."
But he confirmed the shift in attitude from the previous government which promoted unilateral cuts in tariffs.
Howard said: "... no country can ever ignore what others are doing and we won't ignore what others are doing."

Now, while the Prime Minister might have been frustrated about the debate, there are plenty of observers still scratching their heads about the government's real intentions; even more so after the APEC conference when, it seemed, Howard had got the free-trade religion in a big way, something of a contrast with those earlier remarks.
"The purpose of being in APEC is that if we reduce trade barriers in the fastest growing region in the world, that will give direct benefits to the Australian people."
"It will mean more jobs, it will mean higher living standards and it will mean a better future particularly for young Australians -- otherwise I wouldn't be in it."
"You don't join something like that to serve an economic theory."
"I think in the past in governments, and this is not meant to be a criticism of the former Labor government -- it's a generic criticism."
"Governments have not been terribly good at selling the detailed benefits of trade liberalisation."
It was Paul Keating who invented the phrase "APEC equals growth, equals jobs" which drew the admiring line from Bill Clinton: "I couldn't have put it better myself."
But perhaps Howard was right in that Keating didn't promote that regularly enough to sell it to the trade recalcitrants.
But Howard's post-APEC enthusiasm left Keating standing.

"It's easy for those who suffer short-term dislocation to attract attention in complaining about that short-term dislocation and I am sympathetic to that but the concommitant obligation that is put on governments to point out the advantages of liberalisation," he said.

"One of the things I am certainly going to do as a result of this meeting is to step up the explanation to the Australian public and step up the communication to the Australian public of the benefits of globalisation because there are great benefits."
Not a mention of reciprocity.
No caution there.
After a day in a pineapple fibre shirt, Howard was on the free trade cart and wielding the whip.
The Pauline Hansons of this world will not welcome the shift.
The pesky Independent member for Oxley is already promising to whip up trouble over one of Australia's APEC promises -- to remove restrictions on foreign real estate purchases.

While Howard is convinced he can sell the benefits of free trade, he's got a difficult job ahead of him selling it to the broad range of industry, particularly pockets of manufacturing already complaining of the impact of imports.
If there's some confusion about just how free is Howard's trade policy, there are deeper misgivings about the coalition's industry policy.
There are plenty of industry groups who will tell you they don't believe the government actually has an industry policy.
Industry Minister John Moore is committed to sectoral intervention.
But all the sectors have seen so far are cuts in assistance -- A$3 billion over four years -- including the emasculation of the syndicated research and development grants.
And now TNT's David Mortimer will conduct an audit of the remaining A$2.3 billion worth of industry assistance.
As far as many industry bodies are concerned this is a front for more cuts.
-- Reuters Canberra bureau 61-6 273-2730
